usage_en: Used to politely request something or place an order.

examples.en: Water, please.
Please give me the menu.
Please give me the receipt.

usage_en: Used to ask what something is when you don't know its name or identity.

examples.en: What is this?
What is that food?
What is this word?

usage_en: Used to ask whether something exists or is available.

examples.en: Is there Wi-Fi?
Do you have an English menu?
Is there an empty seat?

usage_en: Used to ask for directions to a place.

examples.en: How do I get to Seoul Station?
How do I get to City Hall?
How do I get to the airport?

usage_en: Used to say that you want to go to a place.

examples.en: I want to go to the Han River.
I want to go to Busan.
I want to go home.

usage_en: Say what food you want to eat right now. Just place a noun before 먹고 싶어요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 삼겹살 먹고 싶어요. (I want to eat samgyeopsal.) or 냉면 먹고 싶어요. (I want to eat naengmyeon.).

examples.en: I want to eat samgyeopsal.
I want to eat naengmyeon.
I want to eat tteokbokki.

usage_en: Say what you cannot eat due to allergy or preference. Say what you need, then add 못 먹어요 at the end. Common uses: 매운 거 못 먹어요. (I can't eat spicy food.) or 조개 못 먹어요. (I can't eat shellfish.).

examples.en: I can't eat spicy food.
I can't eat shellfish.
I can't eat dairy products.

usage_en: Decide on one option when ordering or choosing. Just place a noun before 로 할게요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 이걸로 할게요. (I'll go with this one.) or 아메리카노로 할게요. (I'll have the Americano.).

examples.en: I'll go with this one.
I'll have the Americano.
I'll take the large size.

usage_en: Ask permission before eating something. Just place a noun before 먹어도 돼요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 이거 먹어도 돼요? (Is it okay to eat this?) or 여기서 먹어도 돼요? (Is it okay to eat here?).

examples.en: Is it okay to eat this?
Is it okay to eat here?
Is it okay to eat all of this?

usage_en: Ask if someone has ever experienced something before. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 한국 음식 먹어 본 적 있어요? (Have you ever tried Korean food?) or 서울에 가 본 적 있어요? (Have you ever been to Seoul?).

examples.en: Have you ever tried Korean food?
examples.ko: 한국 음식 먹어 본 적 있어요?

examples.en: Have you ever been to Seoul?
Have you ever made kimchi?

usage_en: Ask someone to give you a recommendation. Just place a noun before 추천해 주세요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 메뉴 추천해 주세요. (Please recommend something from the menu.) or 숙소 추천해 주세요. (Please recommend a place to stay.).

examples.en: Please recommend something from the menu.
Please recommend a place to stay.
Please recommend a tourist spot.

usage_en: Politely request someone to do something for you. Say what you need, then add 주실 수 있어요 at the end. Common uses: 사진 찍어 주실 수 있어요? (Could you take a photo for me?) or 도와주실 수 있어요? (Could you help me?).

examples.en: Could you take a photo for me?
Could you help me?
Could you say that again?

usage_en: Say what you like or enjoy. Say what you need, then add 좋아해요 at the end. Common uses: 한국 음식 좋아해요. (I like Korean food.) or 케이팝 좋아해요. (I like K-pop.).

examples.en: I like Korean food.
I like K-pop.
I like cats.

usage_en: Ask permission to call someone by a certain name. Just place a noun before 불러도 돼요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 언니라고 불러도 돼요? (Is it okay to call you 언니?) or 오빠라고 불러도 돼요? (Is it okay to call you 오빠?).

examples.en: Is it okay to call you 언니?
Is it okay to call you 오빠?
Is it okay to call you by your name?

usage_en: Say you'd like to come back to a place again. Just place a noun before 또 오고 싶어요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 여기 또 오고 싶어요. (I want to come here again.) or 한국에 또 오고 싶어요. (I want to come back to Korea.).

examples.en: I want to come here again.
I want to come back to Korea.
I want to come to this restaurant again.

usage_en: Express that something is surprisingly fascinating or unique. Say what you need, then add 신기해요 at the end. Common uses: 이 음식 신기해요. (This food is fascinating.) or 한국 문화가 신기해요. (Korean culture is really fascinating.).

examples.en: This food is fascinating.
Korean culture is really fascinating.
This machine is so cool.

usage_en: Ask if someone has ever tried using something. Say what you need, then add 써봤어요 at the end. Common uses: 이 앱 써봤어요? (Have you tried this app?) or 이 크림 써봤어요? (Have you tried this cream?).

examples.en: Have you tried this app?
Have you tried this cream?
Have you tried Korean cosmetics?

usage_en: Ask which option someone prefers. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 어떤 색이 좋아요? (Which color do you like?) or 어떤 맛이 좋아요? (Which flavor do you like?).

examples.en: Which color do you like?
Which flavor do you like?
Which one do you like among these?

usage_en: Say something is more or less than you expected. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 생각보다 맛있어요. (It's tastier than I expected.) or 생각보다 멀어요. (It's farther than I thought.).

examples.en: It's tastier than I expected.
It's farther than I thought.
It's faster than I expected.

literal_en: I'm so happy we're all together
usage_en: Express happiness that everyone is gathered together. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 다 같이 있어서 정말 좋아요. (I'm so happy we're all together.) or 오늘 다 같이 있어서 좋아요. (I'm glad we're all together today.).

examples.en: I'm so happy we're all together.
I'm glad we're all together today.
I love that we all traveled here together.

usage_en: Say you feel nervous or excited about something important. Just place a noun before 떨려요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 너무 떨려요. (I'm so nervous.) or 첫날이라 떨려요. (I'm nervous because it's the first day.).

examples.en: I'm so nervous.
I'm nervous because it's the first day.
I'm nervous because I have a presentation.

usage_en: Say which country or city you come from. Just place a noun before 에서 왔어요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 미국에서 왔어요. (I'm from the United States.) or 영국에서 왔어요. (I'm from the United Kingdom.).

examples.en: I'm from the United States.
I'm from the United Kingdom.
I'm from Japan.

usage_en: Use when meeting someone to ask for their cooperation. Say what you need, then add 잘 부탁드려요 at the end. Common uses: 처음 뵙겠습니다. 잘 부탁드려요. (Nice to meet you. Please take good care of me.) or 앞으로 잘 부탁드려요. (Please take good care of me going forward.).

examples.en: Nice to meet you. Please take good care of me.
Please take good care of me going forward.
We'll be working together. Please take care of me.

usage_en: Say which mode of transport you are taking. Just place a noun before 타요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 지하철 타요. (I take the subway.) or 버스 타요. (I take the bus.).

examples.en: I take the subway.
I take the bus.
I take a taxi.

usage_en: Say where you get off a bus or subway. Say what you need, then add 에서 내려요 at the end. Common uses: 다음 정류장에서 내려요. (I get off at the next stop.) or 서울역에서 내려요. (I get off at Seoul Station.).

examples.en: I get off at the next stop.
I get off at Seoul Station.
I get off here.

usage_en: Tell a driver where you want to be taken. Just place a noun before 까지 가 주세요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 공항까지 가 주세요. (Please take me to the airport.) or 명동까지 가 주세요. (Please take me to Myeongdong.).

examples.en: Please take me to the airport.
Please take me to Myeongdong.
Please take me to the hotel.

usage_en: Ask for food to be prepared with less of a certain quality. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 덜 맵게 해 주세요. (Please make it less spicy.) or 덜 달게 해 주세요. (Please make it less sweet.).

examples.en: Please make it less spicy.
Please make it less sweet.
Please make it less salty.

usage_en: Ask if a food or drink can be refilled for free. Just place a noun before 리필 돼요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 음료 리필 돼요? (Can I get a refill on the drink?) or 커피 리필 돼요? (Is coffee refillable?).

examples.en: Can I get a refill on the drink?
Is coffee refillable?
Can I get more rice?

usage_en: Ask what someone is doing at a time or place. Just place a noun before 에 뭐 해요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 주말에 뭐 해요? (What do you do on weekends?) or 오늘 저녁에 뭐 해요? (What are you doing tonight?).

examples.en: What do you do on weekends?
What are you doing tonight?
What are you doing here?

usage_en: Invite someone to do something together with you. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 같이 밥 먹을래요? (Do you want to eat together?) or 같이 갈래요? (Do you want to go together?).

examples.en: Do you want to eat together?
Do you want to go together?
Do you want to have coffee together?

usage_en: Tell someone you are going to be a little late. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 조금 늦을 것 같아요, 미안해요. (I think I'll be a little late, I'm sorry.) or 길이 막혀서 조금 늦을 것 같아요. (There's traffic, so I think I'll be a little late.).

examples.en: I think I'll be a little late, I'm sorry.
There's traffic, so I think I'll be a little late.
examples.ko: 길이 막혀서 조금 늦을 것 같아요.

examples.en: I think I'll be about 10 minutes late.

usage_en: Tell someone you are lost and need directions. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 길을 잃었어요, 도와주세요. (I'm lost, please help me.) or 지도가 없어서 길을 잃었어요. (I got lost because I don't have a map.).

examples.en: I'm lost, please help me.
I got lost because I don't have a map.
I got lost while looking for the subway station.

usage_en: Tell someone to simply go straight ahead. Say what you need, then add 쭉 가면 돼요 at the end. Common uses: 이 길로 쭉 가면 돼요. (Just go straight down this road.) or 쭉 가면 돼요, 어렵지 않아요. (Just go straight, it's not difficult.).

examples.en: Just go straight down this road.
Just go straight, it's not difficult.
Just go straight all the way to over there.

usage_en: Tell someone which direction to turn. Just place a noun before 으로 꺾으면 돼요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 왼쪽으로 꺾으면 돼요. (Just turn left.) or 오른쪽으로 꺾으면 돼요. (Just turn right.).

examples.en: Just turn left.
Just turn right.
Just turn right at that corner.

usage_en: Ask if someone has seen or watched something. Say what you need, then add 봤어요 at the end. Common uses: 이 영화 봤어요? (Have you seen this movie?) or 오징어게임 봤어요? (Have you seen Squid Game?).

examples.en: Have you seen this movie?
Have you seen Squid Game?
Did you see the news?

usage_en: Say that something is fun or interesting. Say what you need, then add 재미있어요 at the end. Common uses: 이 게임 재미있어요. (This game is fun.) or 한국어 공부가 재미있어요. (Studying Korean is fun.).

examples.en: This game is fun.
Studying Korean is fun.
This movie is really interesting.

usage_en: Strongly recommend something you found great. Say what you need, then add 강추예요 at the end. Common uses: 이 식당 강추예요! (I strongly recommend this restaurant!) or 이 영화 강추예요. (I highly recommend this movie.).

examples.en: I strongly recommend this restaurant!
I highly recommend this movie.
I strongly recommend this place, you must visit.
examples.ko: 이 곳 강추예요, 꼭 가 보세요.

usage_en: Ask about the weather in a place or at a time. Just place a noun before 날씨 어때요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 서울 날씨 어때요? (How's the weather in Seoul?) or 요즘 날씨 어때요? (How's the weather lately?).

examples.en: How's the weather in Seoul?
How's the weather lately?
How's the weather tomorrow?

usage_en: Say it looks like rain, snow, or something is coming. Just place a noun before 올 것 같아요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 비 올 것 같아요. (It looks like it's going to rain.) or 눈 올 것 같아요. (It looks like it's going to snow.).

examples.en: It looks like it's going to rain.
It looks like it's going to snow.
It looks like a typhoon is coming.

usage_en: Say you need to prepare or bring something with you. Just place a noun before 챙겨야겠어요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 우산 챙겨야겠어요. (I need to bring an umbrella.) or 따뜻하게 챙겨야겠어요. (I need to dress warmly.).

examples.en: I need to bring an umbrella.
I need to dress warmly.
I need to bring medicine.

usage_en: Say which body part is hurting. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 배가 아파요. (My stomach hurts.) or 머리가 아파요. (My head hurts.).

examples.en: My stomach hurts.
My head hurts.
My throat hurts.

usage_en: Ask if there is medicine for a specific ailment. Just place a noun before 약 있어요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 두통약 있어요? (Do you have headache medicine?) or 소화제 있어요? (Do you have digestive medicine?).

examples.en: Do you have headache medicine?
Do you have digestive medicine?
Do you have cold medicine?

usage_en: Advise that it is better not to eat something. Say what you need, then add 안 먹는 게 나아요 at the end. Common uses: 매운 거 안 먹는 게 나아요. (It's better not to eat spicy food.) or 지금은 안 먹는 게 나아요. (It's better not to eat right now.).

examples.en: It's better not to eat spicy food.
examples.ko: 매운 거 안 먹는 게 나아요.

examples.en: It's better not to eat right now.
When your stomach hurts, it's better not to eat.
examples.ko: 배 아플 때는 안 먹는 게 나아요.

usage_en: Ask someone what their hobby or interests are. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 취미가 뭐예요? (What is your hobby?) or 요즘 취미가 뭐예요? (What's your hobby these days?).

examples.en: What is your hobby?
What's your hobby these days?
What's your special hobby?

usage_en: Quickly agree by saying you feel the same way. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 저도요! 저도 한국 좋아해요. (Me too! I like Korea too.) or 저도요, 저도 배고파요. (Me too, I'm hungry too.).

examples.en: Me too! I like Korea too.
Me too, I'm hungry too.
Me too! Let's go together.

usage_en: Say something is not great or doesn't meet expectations. Say what you need, then add 별로예요 at the end. Common uses: 이 음식 별로예요. (This food is not great.) or 날씨가 별로예요. (The weather isn't great.).

examples.en: This food is not great.
The weather isn't great.
This movie is not that good.

usage_en: Ask what's famous or popular at a specific place. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 여기서 유명한 게 뭐예요? 음식 추천해 주세요. (What's famous here? Please recommend some food.) or 이 시장에서 유명한 게 뭐예요? (What's famous at this market?).

examples.en: What's famous here? Please recommend some food.
examples.ko: 여기서 유명한 게 뭐예요? 음식 추천해 주세요.

examples.en: What's famous at this market?
What's famous in Jeju Island?

usage_en: Invite someone to take a photo together. Just place a noun before 같이 사진 찍어요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 저랑 같이 사진 찍어요! (Let's take a photo together!) or 여기서 같이 사진 찍어요. 배경이 예뻐요. (Let's take a photo together here. The background is pretty.).

examples.en: Let's take a photo together!
Let's take a photo together here. The background is pretty.
examples.ko: 여기서 같이 사진 찍어요. 배경이 예뻐요.

examples.en: I took a photo together with my friends.

usage_en: Ask if the photo turned out well. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 사진이 잘 나왔어요? 한번 볼게요. (Did the photo come out well? Let me take a look.) or 오늘 사진이 잘 나왔어요! 너무 좋아요. (The photos came out great today! I love them.).

examples.en: Did the photo come out well? Let me take a look.
The photos came out great today! I love them.
examples.ko: 오늘 사진이 잘 나왔어요! 너무 좋아요.

examples.en: There was no light, so the photo didn't come out well.
examples.ko: 빛이 없어서 사진이 잘 안 나왔어요.

usage_en: Greet someone you haven't seen in a while. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 오랜만이에요! 잘 지냈어요? (Long time no see! Have you been well?) or 어, 오랜만이에요. 요즘 어때요? (Oh, long time no see. How have you been lately?).

examples.en: Long time no see! Have you been well?
Oh, long time no see. How have you been lately?
It's really been a while. We're meeting after a whole year.

usage_en: Ask someone how they've been doing. Just place a noun before 잘 지냈어요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 오랜만이에요. 잘 지냈어요? (Long time no see. Have you been well?) or 요즘 잘 지냈어요? 많이 바빴어요? (Have you been well lately? Were you very busy?).

examples.en: Long time no see. Have you been well?
Have you been well lately? Were you very busy?
Yes, I've been doing well. Thank you.

usage_en: A warm goodbye that leaves the door open to meet again. Say what you need, then add 다음에 또 봐요 at the end. Common uses: 오늘 재밌었어요. 다음에 또 봐요! (Today was fun. See you again next time!) or 다음에 또 봐요. 연락할게요. (See you next time. I'll be in touch.).

examples.en: Today was fun. See you again next time!
See you next time. I'll be in touch.
I have to get going — I'm busy. See you again!

usage_en: Casual past tense ending meaning 'I did' or 'it was.' Say what you need, then add 었어 at the end. Common uses: 어제 영화 봤어. 진짜 재밌었어. (I watched a movie yesterday. It was really fun.) or 밥 먹었어. 이제 배불러. (I ate. I'm full now.).

examples.en: I watched a movie yesterday. It was really fun.
I ate. I'm full now.
I was so tired today.

usage_en: Casually ask how something was. Just place a noun before 어땠어 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 여행 어땠어? 재밌었어? (How was the trip? Was it fun?) or 시험 어땠어? 잘 봤어? (How was the exam? Did you do well?).

examples.en: How was the trip? Was it fun?
How was the exam? Did you do well?
How was that restaurant? Was the food good?

usage_en: Say 'it was my first time, but...' to describe a new experience. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 처음이었는데 생각보다 괜찮았어. (It was my first time, but it was better than I expected.) or 스키 처음이었는데 진짜 재밌었어요. (It was my first time skiing, but it was really fun.).

examples.en: It was my first time, but it was better than I expected.
It was my first time skiing, but it was really fun.
It was my first time traveling alone, but I felt so free.

usage_en: Softly express a guess or opinion with 'I think' or 'it seems.' Say what you need, then add 것 같아요 at the end. Common uses: 비가 올 것 같아요. 우산 챙기세요. (I think it's going to rain. Bring an umbrella.) or 이 음식이 맛있을 것 같아요. (I think this food will be delicious.).

examples.en: I think it's going to rain. Bring an umbrella.
examples.ko: 비가 올 것 같아요. 우산 챙기세요.

examples.en: I think this food will be delicious.
I think that movie will be boring.

usage_en: Make a casual inference: 'it seems like' or 'I guess.' Say what you need, then add 나 봐요 at the end. Common uses: 불이 꺼졌어요. 자나 봐요. (The lights are off. They must be sleeping.) or 많이 먹네요. 배가 고프나 봐요. (You're eating a lot. I guess you're hungry.).

examples.en: The lights are off. They must be sleeping.
You're eating a lot. I guess you're hungry.
They keep smiling. It seems they're in a great mood.
examples.ko: 계속 웃고 있어요. 기분이 좋나 봐요.

usage_en: Casual future tense: 'I'm going to' or 'it will.' It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 나 내일 일찍 일어날 거야. (I'm going to wake up early tomorrow.) or 이번 주말에 친구 만날 거야. (I'm going to meet a friend this weekend.).

examples.en: I'm going to wake up early tomorrow.
I'm going to meet a friend this weekend.
I'm going to study hard. I will definitely pass.
examples.ko: 열심히 공부할 거야. 꼭 합격할 거야.

usage_en: Say you have to or must do something. Just place a noun before 해야 해 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 숙제 해야 해. 오늘 안에 끝내야 해. (I have to do homework. I need to finish it today.) or 이제 자야 해. 내일 일찍 일어나야 해. (I need to sleep now. I have to wake up early tomorrow.).

examples.en: I have to do homework. I need to finish it today.
examples.ko: 숙제 해야 해. 오늘 안에 끝내야 해.

examples.en: I need to sleep now. I have to wake up early tomorrow.
examples.ko: 이제 자야 해. 내일 일찍 일어나야 해.

examples.en: I have to go to the hospital. I'm not feeling well.
examples.ko: 병원에 가야 해. 몸이 안 좋아.

usage_en: Tell someone not to do something, casually. Just place a noun before 하지 마 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 걱정하지 마. 다 잘 될 거야. (Don't worry. Everything will be fine.) or 거기 가지 마. 위험해. (Don't go there. It's dangerous.).

examples.en: Don't worry. Everything will be fine.
examples.ko: 걱정하지 마. 다 잘 될 거야.

examples.en: Don't go there. It's dangerous.
Don't say things like that. It hurts.
examples.ko: 그런 말 하지 마. 기분 나빠.

usage_en: Remind someone not to forget something important. Just place a noun before 잊지 마 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 우산 잊지 마. 비 온대. (Don't forget your umbrella. They say it'll rain.) or 내일 약속 잊지 마! (Don't forget our plans tomorrow!).

examples.en: Don't forget your umbrella. They say it'll rain.
Don't forget our plans tomorrow!
Don't forget to take your medicine.

usage_en: Ask for someone's opinion on a specific topic. Say what you need, then add 어떻게 생각해요 at the end. Common uses: 이 아이디어 어떻게 생각해요? (What do you think about this idea?) or 제 발표 어떻게 생각해요? 잘 했어요? (What do you think of my presentation? Did I do well?).

examples.en: What do you think about this idea?
What do you think of my presentation? Did I do well?
examples.ko: 제 발표 어떻게 생각해요? 잘 했어요?

examples.en: What do you think of Korean food?

usage_en: Agree with and validate what someone just said. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 맞는 말이에요. 저도 그렇게 생각해요. (That's true. I think so too.) or 맞는 말이에요! 왜 그걸 몰랐을까요? (You're right! Why didn't I think of that?).

examples.en: That's true. I think so too.
You're right! Why didn't I think of that?
That's absolutely right. Health is the most important thing.
examples.ko: 그거 맞는 말이에요. 건강이 제일 중요하죠.

usage_en: Ask if someone has ever visited a particular place. Just place a noun before 에 가 봤어요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 제주도에 가 봤어요? (Have you ever been to Jeju Island?) or 그 카페에 가 봤어요? 분위기가 좋대요. (Have you been to that café? I heard it has a great atmosphere.).

examples.en: Have you ever been to Jeju Island?
Have you been to that café? I heard it has a great atmosphere.
examples.ko: 그 카페에 가 봤어요? 분위기가 좋대요.

examples.en: Have you been to Gyeongbokgung? It's really beautiful.

usage_en: Strongly recommend that someone visit a place. Say what you need, then add 꼭 가 보세요 at the end. Common uses: 그 식당 꼭 가 보세요. 정말 맛있어요. (You should definitely go to that restaurant. It's really delicious.) or 한국에 오면 부산 꼭 가 보세요. (If you come to Korea, definitely go to Busan.).

examples.en: You should definitely go to that restaurant. It's really delicious.
examples.ko: 그 식당 꼭 가 보세요. 정말 맛있어요.

examples.en: If you come to Korea, definitely go to Busan.
examples.ko: 한국에 오면 부산 꼭 가 보세요.

examples.en: Definitely go see this exhibition. You won't regret it.
examples.ko: 이 전시회 꼭 가 보세요. 후회 안 해요.

usage_en: Ask when someone is free or available to meet. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 언제 시간 돼요? 밥 한번 먹어요. (When are you free? Let's grab a meal.) or 이번 주에 언제 시간 돼요? (When are you available this week?).

examples.en: When are you free? Let's grab a meal.
examples.ko: 언제 시간 돼요? 밥 한번 먹어요.

examples.en: When are you available this week?
When do you have time? I need some help.

usage_en: Ask what shows or content someone is watching these days. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 요즘 뭐 봐요? 재밌는 드라마 있어요? (What are you watching these days? Any good dramas?) or 요즘 뭐 봐요? 추천해 주세요. (What are you watching lately? Please recommend something.).

examples.en: What are you watching these days? Any good dramas?
examples.ko: 요즘 뭐 봐요? 재밌는 드라마 있어요?

examples.en: What are you watching lately? Please recommend something.
I watch YouTube a lot lately. Cooking channels.
examples.ko: 요즘 유튜브 많이 봐요. 요리 채널이요.

usage_en: Say you're totally hooked or obsessed with something. Say what you need, then add 완전 빠져들었어요 at the end. Common uses: 이 드라마에 완전 빠져들었어요. 못 멈춰요. (I'm totally hooked on this drama. I can't stop.) or 요즘 그 게임에 완전 빠져들었어요. (I've been completely absorbed in that game lately.).

examples.en: I'm totally hooked on this drama. I can't stop.
examples.ko: 이 드라마에 완전 빠져들었어요. 못 멈춰요.

examples.en: I've been completely absorbed in that game lately.
I'm totally hooked on studying Korean!

usage_en: Express excitement and anticipation for the next episode. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 다음 화가 너무 기대돼요. 빨리 보고 싶어요. (I'm so excited for the next episode. I want to watch it now.) or 오늘 끝이 충격적이었어요. 다음 화가 기대돼요. (Today's ending was shocking. I can't wait for the next episode.).

examples.en: I'm so excited for the next episode. I want to watch it now.
examples.ko: 다음 화가 너무 기대돼요. 빨리 보고 싶어요.

examples.en: Today's ending was shocking. I can't wait for the next episode.
examples.ko: 오늘 끝이 충격적이었어요. 다음 화가 기대돼요.

examples.en: How am I supposed to wait until next week? I can't wait for the next episode.
examples.ko: 다음 주까지 어떻게 기다려요? 다음 화가 기대돼요.

usage_en: Ask if someone knows or recognizes a particular song. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 이 노래 알아요? 요즘 엄청 유명해요. (Do you know this song? It's really popular these days.) or 이 노래 알아요? 제가 제일 좋아하는 노래예요. (Do you know this song? It's my absolute favorite.).

examples.en: Do you know this song? It's really popular these days.
examples.ko: 이 노래 알아요? 요즘 엄청 유명해요.

examples.en: Do you know this song? It's my absolute favorite.
examples.ko: 이 노래 알아요? 제가 제일 좋아하는 노래예요.

examples.en: Do you know this song? Let's sing it together!

usage_en: Ask what a song's lyrics mean. Say what you need, then add 가사가 무슨 뜻이에요 at the end. Common uses: 이 부분 가사가 무슨 뜻이에요? (What does this part of the lyrics mean?) or 가사가 무슨 뜻이에요? 번역해 줄 수 있어요? (What do the lyrics mean? Can you translate them?).

examples.en: What does this part of the lyrics mean?
What do the lyrics mean? Can you translate them?
examples.ko: 가사가 무슨 뜻이에요? 번역해 줄 수 있어요?

examples.en: The lyrics are so beautiful. What do they mean?

usage_en: Say something is catchy or impossible to stop enjoying. Say what you need, then add 중독성 있어요 at the end. Common uses: 이 노래 중독성 있어요. 계속 듣게 돼요. (This song is so addictive. I keep listening to it on repeat.) or 이 음식 중독성 있어요. 또 먹고 싶어요. (This food is addictive. I want to eat it again already.).

examples.en: This song is so addictive. I keep listening to it on repeat.
examples.ko: 이 노래 중독성 있어요. 계속 듣게 돼요.

examples.en: This food is addictive. I want to eat it again already.
examples.ko: 이 음식 중독성 있어요. 또 먹고 싶어요.

examples.en: This game is really addictive. Be careful.
examples.ko: 이 게임 진짜 중독성 있어요. 조심하세요.

usage_en: Ask how someone takes care of or manages something. Just place a noun before 관리 어떻게 해요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 피부 관리 어떻게 해요? 피부가 너무 좋아요. (How do you take care of your skin? It looks amazing.) or 머리 관리 어떻게 해요? 어떤 제품 써요? (How do you manage your hair? What products do you use?).

examples.en: How do you take care of your skin? It looks amazing.
examples.ko: 피부 관리 어떻게 해요? 피부가 너무 좋아요.

examples.en: How do you manage your hair? What products do you use?
examples.ko: 머리 관리 어떻게 해요? 어떤 제품 써요?

examples.en: How do you manage your health? What's your secret?
examples.ko: 건강 관리 어떻게 해요? 비결이 뭐예요?

usage_en: Ask if something actually works or makes a difference. Say what you need, then add 효과 있어요 at the end. Common uses: 이 크림 효과 있어요? 써 봤어요? (Is this cream effective? Have you tried it?) or 그 다이어트 방법 효과 있어요? (Does that diet method actually work?).

examples.en: Is this cream effective? Have you tried it?
examples.ko: 이 크림 효과 있어요? 써 봤어요?

examples.en: Does that diet method actually work?
Does this medicine work? I want to get better fast.
examples.ko: 이 약 효과 있어요? 빨리 낫고 싶어요.

usage_en: Say the reviews or word-of-mouth for something are great. Say what you need, then add 후기가 좋아요 at the end. Common uses: 이 식당 후기가 좋아요. 한번 가 봐요. (This restaurant has great reviews. Let's try it out.) or 그 제품 후기가 진짜 좋아요. 한번 써 봐요. (That product has really great reviews. Let's give it a try.).

examples.en: This restaurant has great reviews. Let's try it out.
examples.ko: 이 식당 후기가 좋아요. 한번 가 봐요.

examples.en: That product has really great reviews. Let's give it a try.
examples.ko: 그 제품 후기가 진짜 좋아요. 한번 써 봐요.

examples.en: I made a reservation because the reviews were so good.

usage_en: Ask how often someone does a particular activity. Just place a noun before 얼마나 자주 해요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 운동 얼마나 자주 해요? (How often do you exercise?) or 얼마나 자주 해요? 저는 일주일에 세 번 해요. (How often do you do it? I do it three times a week.).

examples.en: How often do you exercise?
How often do you do it? I do it three times a week.
examples.ko: 얼마나 자주 해요? 저는 일주일에 세 번 해요.

examples.en: How often do you clean your place?

usage_en: Say that something is good for your health. Just place a noun before 건강에 좋아요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 녹차는 건강에 좋아요. (Green tea is good for your health.) or 매일 걷는 게 건강에 좋아요. (Walking every day is good for your health.).

examples.en: Green tea is good for your health.
Walking every day is good for your health.
This food is healthy. Please eat plenty of it.
examples.ko: 이 음식이 건강에 좋아요. 많이 드세요.

usage_en: Say you've been keeping up with something consistently. Say what you need, then add 꾸준히 하고 있어요 at the end. Common uses: 매일 운동 꾸준히 하고 있어요. (I've been exercising consistently every day.) or 한국어 공부 꾸준히 하고 있어요. 실력이 늘어요. (I've been studying Korean consistently. My skills are improving.).

examples.en: I've been exercising consistently every day.
I've been studying Korean consistently. My skills are improving.
examples.ko: 한국어 공부 꾸준히 하고 있어요. 실력이 늘어요.

examples.en: I'm keeping at it consistently. I won't give up.
examples.ko: 꾸준히 하고 있어요. 포기하지 않을 거예요.

usage_en: Ask where someone currently lives. Just place a noun before 어디 살아요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 지금 어디 살아요? 서울이에요? (Where do you live now? Is it Seoul?) or 한국 어디 살아요? 회사 근처예요? (Where in Korea do you live? Is it near your workplace?).

examples.en: Where do you live now? Is it Seoul?
Where in Korea do you live? Is it near your workplace?
Where do you live? I hope it's close to me.
examples.ko: 어디 살아요? 저랑 가까운 곳이면 좋겠어요.

usage_en: Ask if someone lives by themselves. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 혼자 살아요? 요리 잘 해요? (Do you live alone? Are you good at cooking?) or 혼자 살아요? 외롭지 않아요? (Do you live alone? Don't you get lonely?).

examples.en: Do you live alone? Are you good at cooking?
Do you live alone? Don't you get lonely?
Yes, I live alone. I like it because I'm free.

usage_en: Casually ask what places or things are near somewhere. Just place a noun before 근처에 뭐 있어 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 집 근처에 뭐 있어? 카페 있어? (What's near your place? Is there a café?) or 학교 근처에 뭐 있어? 밥 먹을 데 있어? (What's near the school? Is there anywhere to eat?).

examples.en: What's near your place? Is there a café?
examples.ko: 집 근처에 뭐 있어? 카페 있어?

examples.en: What's near the school? Is there anywhere to eat?
examples.ko: 학교 근처에 뭐 있어? 밥 먹을 데 있어?

examples.en: Is there a convenience store near there?

usage_en: Ask for someone's opinion about something. Say what you need, then add 어때요 at the end. Common uses: 이 음식 어때요? (How is this food?) or 오늘 날씨 어때요? (How is the weather today?).

examples.en: How is this food?
How is the weather today?
How is this outfit?

usage_en: Ask for more of something you already have. Just place a noun before 더 주세요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 물 더 주세요. (Please give me more water.) or 김치 더 주세요. (Please give me more kimchi.).

examples.en: Please give me more water.
Please give me more kimchi.
Please give me more rice.

usage_en: Politely ask for a lower price on something. Just place a noun before 깎아 주세요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 좀 깎아 주세요. (Please give me a discount.) or 만 원만 깎아 주세요. (Please discount 10,000 won.).

examples.en: Please give me a discount.
Please discount 10,000 won.
Please lower the price a little.

usage_en: Say that something has already been done. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 이미 먹었어요. (I already ate.) or 이미 알아요. (I already know.).

examples.en: I already ate.
I already know.
I already bought it.

usage_en: Ask where to board a specific type of transport. Just place a noun before 어디서 타요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 버스 어디서 타요? (Where do I get on the bus?) or 공항버스 어디서 타요? (Where do I get on the airport bus?).

examples.en: Where do I get on the bus?
Where do I get on the airport bus?
Where do I get on the subway?

usage_en: Politely say you're a bit different or have your own preference. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 저는 좀 달라요. 매운 음식을 못 먹어요. (I'm a bit different. I can't eat spicy food.) or 저는 좀 달라요. 아침형 인간이에요. (I'm a bit different. I'm a morning person.).

examples.en: I'm a bit different. I can't eat spicy food.
examples.ko: 저는 좀 달라요. 매운 음식을 못 먹어요.

examples.en: I'm a bit different. I'm a morning person.
I'm a bit different. I like being alone.
examples.ko: 저는 좀 달라요. 혼자 있는 게 좋아요.

usage_en: Casually check in and ask how someone is feeling. Just place a noun before 기분이 어때 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 오늘 기분이 어때? 좋아 보여. (How are you feeling today? You look happy.) or 기분이 어때? 많이 나아졌어? (How are you feeling? Are you feeling much better?).

examples.en: How are you feeling today? You look happy.
How are you feeling? Are you feeling much better?
How are you feeling? You look like something's wrong.
examples.ko: 기분이 어때? 표정이 안 좋아 보여.

usage_en: Express happiness by stating the reason with 'because.' It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 네가 옆에 있어서 행복해. (I'm happy because you're by my side.) or 오늘 날씨가 좋아서 행복해. (I'm happy because the weather is so nice today.).

examples.en: I'm happy because you're by my side.
I'm happy because the weather is so nice today.
I'm happy because I ate something delicious!

usage_en: Describe that fluttery, giddy feeling of excited anticipation. Say what you need, then add 설레 at the end. Common uses: 내일 여행 가는데 너무 설레! (I'm going on a trip tomorrow and I'm so excited!) or 처음 만나는 거라 설레요. (I'm nervous and excited because it's our first time meeting.).

examples.en: I'm going on a trip tomorrow and I'm so excited!
I'm nervous and excited because it's our first time meeting.
The new semester has started. I feel excited and nervous at the same time.

usage_en: Check in to make sure someone is okay. Say what you need, then add 괜찮아요 at the end. Common uses: 얼굴이 안 좋아 보여요. 괜찮아요? (You don't look well. Are you okay?) or 넘어졌어요? 괜찮아요? 다쳤어요? (Did you fall? Are you okay? Are you hurt?).

examples.en: You don't look well. Are you okay?
Did you fall? Are you okay? Are you hurt?
It must be tough. Are you doing okay?

usage_en: Share honestly that things have been a bit tough lately. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 요즘 좀 힘들어요. 일이 너무 많아요. (Things have been a bit tough lately. I have so much work.) or 요즘 좀 힘들어요. 잠을 못 자고 있어요. (I've been struggling a bit lately. I can't sleep well.).

examples.en: Things have been a bit tough lately. I have so much work.
examples.ko: 요즘 좀 힘들어요. 일이 너무 많아요.

examples.en: I've been struggling a bit lately. I can't sleep well.
examples.ko: 요즘 좀 힘들어요. 잠을 못 자고 있어요.

examples.en: Things are a bit hard lately, but I'm still hanging in there.

usage_en: Tell someone they can reach out to you any time. Say what you need, then add 언제든지 연락해요 at the end. Common uses: 도움 필요하면 언제든지 연락해요. (If you need help, contact me anytime.) or 언제든지 연락해요. 항상 여기 있어요. (Reach out anytime. I'm always here.).

examples.en: If you need help, contact me anytime.
Reach out anytime. I'm always here.
If things get hard, contact me anytime. Let's talk together.

usage_en: Ask if someone uses KakaoTalk to swap contact info. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 카카오톡 해요? 아이디 알려줄게요. (Do you use KakaoTalk? I'll give you my ID.) or 카카오톡 해요? 거기서 연락해요. (Are you on KakaoTalk? Let's keep in touch there.).

examples.en: Do you use KakaoTalk? I'll give you my ID.
Are you on KakaoTalk? Let's keep in touch there.
Do you use KakaoTalk? Let's make a group chat.

usage_en: Politely ask permission to follow someone on social media. Just place a noun before 팔로우해도 돼요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 인스타그램 팔로우해도 돼요? (Can I follow you on Instagram?) or 팔로우해도 돼요? 사진이 너무 예뻐요. (Can I follow you? Your photos are so beautiful.).

examples.en: Can I follow you on Instagram?
Can I follow you? Your photos are so beautiful.
Can I follow you? Is your account public?

usage_en: Express that you want to make Korean friends. Say what you need, then add 한국 친구 사귀고 싶어요 at the end. Common uses: 한국어 배우는데 한국 친구 사귀고 싶어요. (I'm learning Korean and I really want to make Korean friends.) or 한국 친구 사귀고 싶어요. 언어 교환 해요? (I want to make Korean friends. Shall we do a language exchange?).

examples.en: I'm learning Korean and I really want to make Korean friends.
examples.ko: 한국어 배우는데 한국 친구 사귀고 싶어요.

examples.en: I want to make Korean friends. Shall we do a language exchange?
examples.ko: 한국 친구 사귀고 싶어요. 언어 교환 해요?

examples.en: I want to make Korean friends. Let's hang out!
examples.ko: 한국 친구 사귀고 싶어요. 같이 놀아요!

usage_en: Offer to treat someone by saying 'it's on me.' Just place a noun before 제가 살게요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 오늘은 제가 살게요. 지난번에 사 줬잖아요. (It's on me today. You treated me last time.) or 제가 살게요! 걱정하지 마세요. (I'll pay! Don't worry about it.).

examples.en: It's on me today. You treated me last time.
examples.ko: 오늘은 제가 살게요. 지난번에 사 줬잖아요.

examples.en: I'll pay! Don't worry about it.
Since it's your birthday, I'll treat you.

usage_en: Ask if everyone is splitting the bill equally. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 더치페이 해요? 각자 내요? (Shall we split the bill? Are we each paying our own?) or 더치페이 해요, 아니면 제가 살게요? (Shall we go Dutch, or should I treat?).

examples.en: Shall we split the bill? Are we each paying our own?
Shall we go Dutch, or should I treat?
Let's split the bill. That's easier.

usage_en: Casually suggest grabbing a meal together sometime. Say what you need, then add 밥 한번 먹어요 at the end. Common uses: 시간 될 때 밥 한번 먹어요. (Let's grab a meal together when you have time.) or 오랜만인데 밥 한번 먹어요! (It's been a while — let's get a meal together!).

examples.en: Let's grab a meal together when you have time.
examples.ko: 시간 될 때 밥 한번 먹어요.

examples.en: It's been a while — let's get a meal together!
If you're in the area, let's grab a meal.

usage_en: Suggest ordering food delivery instead of going out. Say what you need, then add 배달 시켜요 at the end. Common uses: 밖에 나가기 싫어요. 배달 시켜요. (I don't want to go out. Let's order delivery.) or 배달 시켜요. 뭐 먹고 싶어요? (Let's order delivery. What do you want to eat?).

examples.en: I don't want to go out. Let's order delivery.
Let's order delivery. What do you want to eat?
It's raining — let's just order delivery.

usage_en: Casually ask if someone has ever tried wearing something. Say what you need, then add 입어 봤어 at the end. Common uses: 이 옷 입어 봤어? 너한테 잘 어울릴 것 같아. (Have you tried this on? I think it'll suit you really well.) or 한복 입어 봤어? 정말 예뻐. (Have you ever worn a hanbok? It's really beautiful.).

examples.en: Have you tried this on? I think it'll suit you really well.
examples.ko: 이 옷 입어 봤어? 너한테 잘 어울릴 것 같아.

examples.en: Have you ever worn a hanbok? It's really beautiful.
Have you tried wearing that brand's clothes? How was it?
examples.ko: 그 브랜드 옷 입어 봤어? 어땠어?

usage_en: Ask what someone does or plans for Korean holidays. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 추석에 뭐 해? 가족이랑 같이 있어? (What do you do on Chuseok? Are you spending it with family?) or 명절에 뭐 해? 고향에 가? (What do you do on holidays? Do you go to your hometown?).

examples.en: What do you do on Chuseok? Are you spending it with family?
examples.ko: 추석에 뭐 해? 가족이랑 같이 있어?

examples.en: What do you do on holidays? Do you go to your hometown?
What do you do on Seollal? Do you eat tteokguk?

usage_en: Ask a friend casually what a word or expression means. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 이게 무슨 뜻이야? 처음 보는 단어야. (What does this mean? I've never seen this word before.) or 이 노래 가사 이게 무슨 뜻이야? (What does this song lyric mean?).

examples.en: What does this mean? I've never seen this word before.
examples.ko: 이게 무슨 뜻이야? 처음 보는 단어야.

examples.en: What does this song lyric mean?
examples.ko: 이 노래 가사 이게 무슨 뜻이야?

examples.en: I got this text — what does it mean?
examples.ko: 이 문자 받았는데, 이게 무슨 뜻이야?

usage_en: Ask someone politely if they drink alcohol. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 술 마셔요? 같이 한잔할까요? (Do you drink? Want to grab a drink together?) or 저는 술 안 마셔요. 주스 주세요. (I don't drink. Please give me juice.).

examples.en: Do you drink? Want to grab a drink together?
I don't drink. Please give me juice.
examples.ko: 저는 술 안 마셔요. 주스 주세요.

examples.en: Do you drink, or shall we get soft drinks?

usage_en: Say cheers and raise your glass together. Say what you need, then add 건배해요 at the end. Common uses: 모두 다 모였으니까 건배해요! (Everyone's here, so let's toast!) or 생일 축하해서 건배해요. (Let's toast to celebrate your birthday.).

examples.en: Everyone's here, so let's toast!
Let's toast to celebrate your birthday.
Let's toast for the new year!

usage_en: Politely wrap up a session or activity for the day. Say what you need, then add 오늘은 여기까지만 해요 at the end. Common uses: 많이 피곤하죠? 오늘은 여기까지만 해요. (You're tired, right? Let's stop here for today.) or 시간이 됐으니까 오늘은 여기까지만 해요. (Time's up, so let's call it a day here.).

examples.en: You're tired, right? Let's stop here for today.
Time's up, so let's call it a day here.
Let's stop studying here for today. We'll continue tomorrow.
examples.ko: 공부는 오늘은 여기까지만 해요. 내일 또 해요.

usage_en: Invite someone to sing a song together with you. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 이 노래 같이 불러요! 아는 노래예요? (Let's sing this song together! Do you know it?) or 제가 좋아하는 노래예요. 이 노래 같이 불러요. (This is my favorite song. Let's sing it together.).

examples.en: Let's sing this song together! Do you know it?
examples.ko: 이 노래 같이 불러요! 아는 노래예요?

examples.en: This is my favorite song. Let's sing it together.
examples.ko: 제가 좋아하는 노래예요. 이 노래 같이 불러요.

examples.en: Let's sing this song together at karaoke!

usage_en: Ask if someone has a song they'd like to request. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 신청곡 있어요? 뭐든지 틀어드릴게요. (Do you have a song request? I'll play anything you want.) or DJ한테 신청곡 있어요? (Do you have a song request for the DJ?).

examples.en: Do you have a song request? I'll play anything you want.
Do you have a song request for the DJ?
Do you have a song request? I'll sing it for you.

usage_en: Suggest doing just one more song before finishing. Just place a noun before 한 곡 더 해요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 재미있는데 한 곡 더 해요! (This is fun — let's do one more song!) or 시간 있어요? 한 곡 더 해요. (Do you have time? Let's do one more song.).

examples.en: This is fun — let's do one more song!
Do you have time? Let's do one more song.
examples.ko: 시간 있어요? 한 곡 더 해요.

examples.en: Let's do just one more song as the last one.

usage_en: Invite someone to get up and dance with you. Say what you need, then add 같이 춰요 at the end. Common uses: 음악이 좋은데, 같이 춰요! (The music is great — let's dance together!) or 저 춤 잘 못 추는데, 같이 춰요? (I'm not a great dancer, but shall we dance together?).

examples.en: The music is great — let's dance together!
I'm not a great dancer, but shall we dance together?
examples.ko: 저 춤 잘 못 추는데, 같이 춰요?

examples.en: When this song comes on, let's dance together!

usage_en: Express that something is challenging but genuinely enjoyable. Say what you need, then add 어렵지만 재미있어요 at the end. Common uses: 한국어 공부가 어렵지만 재미있어요. (Studying Korean is difficult but fun.) or 이 게임 어렵지만 재미있어요. 계속 하고 싶어요. (This game is hard but fun. I want to keep playing.).

examples.en: Studying Korean is difficult but fun.
This game is hard but fun. I want to keep playing.
examples.ko: 이 게임 어렵지만 재미있어요. 계속 하고 싶어요.

examples.en: Cooking is difficult but really interesting.

usage_en: Encourage someone that consistent practice leads to improvement. Say what you need, then add 하다 보면 늘어요 at the end. Common uses: 걱정하지 마요. 하다 보면 늘어요. (Don't worry. You'll get better as you keep at it.) or 한국어는 하다 보면 늘어요. 포기하지 마세요. (Your Korean will improve if you keep practicing. Don't give up.).

examples.en: Don't worry. You'll get better as you keep at it.
Your Korean will improve if you keep practicing. Don't give up.
examples.ko: 한국어는 하다 보면 늘어요. 포기하지 마세요.

examples.en: It's hard at first, but you'll improve as you go.

usage_en: Compliment the vibe or atmosphere of a place. Say what you need, then add 분위기 좋아요 at the end. Common uses: 이 카페 분위기 좋아요. 자주 와요? (This café has a great vibe. Do you come here often?) or 오늘 파티 분위기 좋아요! (The atmosphere at today's party is great!).

examples.en: This café has a great vibe. Do you come here often?
examples.ko: 이 카페 분위기 좋아요. 자주 와요?

examples.en: The atmosphere at today's party is great!
The music is nice here and the atmosphere is great.

usage_en: Ask if there's something sweet available to eat or drink. Just place a noun before 달달한 거 있어요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 배고픈데 달달한 거 있어요? (I'm hungry — do you have something sweet?) or 커피 말고 달달한 거 있어요? (Aside from coffee, do you have anything sweet?).

examples.en: I'm hungry — do you have something sweet?
Aside from coffee, do you have anything sweet?
I'm stressed. Do you have something sweet?

usage_en: Politely ask whether it's okay to stay for a long time. Say what you need, then add 오래 있어도 돼요 at the end. Common uses: 이 카페 오래 있어도 돼요? (Is it okay to stay at this café for a long time?) or 여기 오래 있어도 돼요? 공부하고 싶어서요. (Can I stay here a long time? I want to study.).

examples.en: Is it okay to stay at this café for a long time?
Can I stay here a long time? I want to study.
examples.ko: 여기 오래 있어도 돼요? 공부하고 싶어서요.

examples.en: We have a lot more to talk about — can we stay longer?
examples.ko: 아직 이야기가 많은데, 오래 있어도 돼요?

usage_en: Point out that customs or practices differ by country. Say what you need, then add 나라마다 달라요 at the end. Common uses: 인사하는 방법이 나라마다 달라요. (The way you greet people differs by country.) or 음식 문화가 나라마다 달라요. (Food culture is different in every country.).

examples.en: The way you greet people differs by country.
Food culture is different in every country.
Wedding customs differ from country to country.

usage_en: Say you've finally adjusted and settled into a new situation. Say what you need, then add 이제 적응이 됐어요 at the end. Common uses: 한국 생활에 이제 적응이 됐어요. (I've finally adjusted to life in Korea.) or 처음엔 힘들었는데 이제 적응이 됐어요. (It was hard at first, but I've gotten used to it now.).

examples.en: I've finally adjusted to life in Korea.
It was hard at first, but I've gotten used to it now.
I've now adjusted to my new job.

usage_en: Start a story by saying something felt strange or unfamiliar at first. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 처음엔 낯설었는데 이제는 괜찮아요. (It felt unfamiliar at first, but it's fine now.) or 한국 음식이 처음엔 낯설었는데 지금은 좋아요. (Korean food was strange to me at first, but I love it now.).

examples.en: It felt unfamiliar at first, but it's fine now.
Korean food was strange to me at first, but I love it now.
examples.ko: 한국 음식이 처음엔 낯설었는데 지금은 좋아요.

examples.en: We felt awkward at first, but now we're close friends.
examples.ko: 처음엔 낯설었는데 이제 친한 친구가 됐어요.

usage_en: Connect two ideas or give soft background context before your point. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 배가 고픈데 뭐 먹을까요? (I'm hungry — what should we eat?) or 오늘 바쁜데 내일 만날 수 있어요? (I'm busy today — can we meet tomorrow?).

examples.en: I'm hungry — what should we eat?
I'm busy today — can we meet tomorrow?
examples.ko: 오늘 바쁜데 내일 만날 수 있어요?

examples.en: I'm studying Korean, but it's difficult.

literal_en: I can't drink. I have to drive, you ~
usage_en: Add an explanation or reason for what you just said. Say what you need, then add 거든 at the end. Common uses: 저 술 못 마셔요. 운전해야 하거든요. (I can't drink. I have to drive, you see.) or 한국어 잘해요. 2년 동안 공부했거든요. (My Korean is good. I studied for two years, you see.).

examples.en: I can't drink. I have to drive, you see.
examples.ko: 저 술 못 마셔요. 운전해야 하거든요.

examples.en: My Korean is good. I studied for two years, you see.
I come to this café often. It's right in front of my home, you see.
examples.ko: 이 카페 자주 와요. 집 앞이거든요.

usage_en: Express surprise or a fresh realization in a natural, casual way. Say what you need, then add 네 at the end. Common uses: 한국어가 생각보다 쉽네요. (Korean is easier than I thought.) or 여기 음식이 정말 맛있네요. (Oh, the food here is really delicious.).

examples.en: Korean is easier than I thought.
Oh, the food here is really delicious.
Oh, it's already gotten this late.

usage_en: Politely suggest an idea or alternative to someone. Say what you need, then add 면 어때요 at the end. Common uses: 내일 만나면 어때요? (How about meeting tomorrow?) or 한국어로 얘기하면 어때요? 연습이 될 거예요. (How about talking in Korean? It'll be good practice.).

examples.en: How about meeting tomorrow?
How about talking in Korean? It'll be good practice.
examples.ko: 한국어로 얘기하면 어때요? 연습이 될 거예요.

examples.en: How about eating together?

literal_en: I hope the weather is nice ~
usage_en: Express a gentle wish or hope about a situation. Say what you need, then add 면 좋겠어요 at the end. Common uses: 내일 날씨가 좋으면 좋겠어요. (I hope the weather is nice tomorrow.) or 한국어가 빨리 늘면 좋겠어요. (I wish my Korean would improve quickly.).

examples.en: I hope the weather is nice tomorrow.
I wish my Korean would improve quickly.
It would be wonderful if we could travel together.

usage_en: Tell someone the only thing they need to do is one simple action. Say what you need, then add 면 돼요 at the end. Common uses: 이 버스 타면 돼요. 어렵지 않아요. (You just need to take this bus. It's not hard.) or 여기에 이름 쓰면 돼요. (You just need to write your name here.).

examples.en: You just need to take this bus. It's not hard.
examples.ko: 이 버스 타면 돼요. 어렵지 않아요.

examples.en: You just need to write your name here.
You just need to press the button once.

literal_en: I couldn't go out because of the ~
usage_en: State the cause or reason for something using 'because of.' Just place a noun before 때문에 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 비 때문에 못 나갔어요. (I couldn't go out because of the rain.) or 일 때문에 요즘 너무 바빠요. (I'm really busy these days because of work.).

examples.en: I couldn't go out because of the rain.
I'm really busy these days because of work.
I started studying Korean because of you.

literal_en: Thanks to my teacher, my Korean has ~
usage_en: Credit someone or something for a positive outcome. Just place a noun before 덕분에 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 선생님 덕분에 한국어 실력이 늘었어요. (Thanks to my teacher, my Korean has improved.) or 친구 덕분에 좋은 식당을 알게 됐어요. (Thanks to my friend, I discovered a great restaurant.).

examples.en: Thanks to my teacher, my Korean has improved.
Thanks to my friend, I discovered a great restaurant.
examples.ko: 친구 덕분에 좋은 식당을 알게 됐어요.

examples.en: Thanks to everyone, I had a wonderful time.

usage_en: Compare two things, saying one is more or less than the other. Say what you need, then add 보다 at the end. Common uses: 한국어가 생각보다 어려워요. (Korean is harder than I thought.) or 서울이 도쿄보다 물가가 저렴해요. (Seoul is cheaper than Tokyo.).

examples.en: Korean is harder than I thought.
Seoul is cheaper than Tokyo.
This bag is lighter than that one.

literal_en: Shall we have coffee while we ~?
usage_en: Describe what happens or happened during a period of time. Just place a noun before 는 동안 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 기다리는 동안 커피 마실까요? (Shall we have coffee while we wait?) or 출근하는 동안 팟캐스트 들어요. (I listen to podcasts while commuting to work.).

examples.en: Shall we have coffee while we wait?
I listen to podcasts while commuting to work.
I learned a lot of Korean while I was in Korea.
examples.ko: 한국에 있는 동안 한국어를 많이 배웠어요.

literal_en: Shall we take a walk after ~?
usage_en: Describe what you do or did after finishing an action. Say what you need, then add 고 나서 at the end. Common uses: 밥 먹고 나서 산책할까요? (Shall we take a walk after eating?) or 샤워하고 나서 전화할게요. (I'll call you after I shower.).

examples.en: Shall we take a walk after eating?
I'll call you after I shower.
Let's eat together after work is done.
examples.ko: 일 끝나고 나서 같이 밥 먹어요.

literal_en: Don't look at your phone before ~
usage_en: Say what you do or should do before a certain action. Just place a noun before 기 전에 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 자기 전에 핸드폰 보지 마세요. (Don't look at your phone before sleeping.) or 밥 먹기 전에 손 씻어요. (Wash your hands before eating.).

examples.en: Don't look at your phone before sleeping.
Wash your hands before eating.
Check the weather before leaving.

usage_en: Offer to do something as a favor for someone. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 제가 도와 줄게요. 걱정하지 마세요. (I'll help you. Don't worry.) or 짐 들어 줄게요. 무거워 보여요. (I'll carry your bag. It looks heavy.).

examples.en: I'll help you. Don't worry.
I'll carry your bag. It looks heavy.
I'll explain it to you. Listen carefully.

usage_en: Politely offer to do something for someone, especially a stranger. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 사진 찍어 드릴까요? (Shall I take a photo for you?) or 문 열어 드릴까요? (Shall I open the door for you?).

examples.en: Shall I take a photo for you?
Shall I open the door for you?
Shall I explain it for you? Is this your first time?

usage_en: Politely interrupt a stranger to ask a question or small favor. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 죄송한데요 혹시 지하철역이 어디예요? (Excuse me, could you tell me where the subway station is?) or 죄송한데요 혹시 사진 찍어 주실 수 있어요? (Excuse me, could you possibly take a photo for us?).

examples.en: Excuse me, could you tell me where the subway station is?
Excuse me, could you possibly take a photo for us?
examples.ko: 죄송한데요 혹시 사진 찍어 주실 수 있어요?

examples.en: Excuse me, is there possibly a seat available?

literal_en: How long has it been since you came to ~?
usage_en: Ask how long it has been since something started or happened. Say what you need, then add 지 얼마나 됐어요 at the end. Common uses: 한국에 온 지 얼마나 됐어요? (How long has it been since you came to Korea?) or 한국어 공부한 지 얼마나 됐어요? (How long have you been studying Korean?).

examples.en: How long has it been since you came to Korea?
How long have you been studying Korean?
How long have you been working at this company?
examples.ko: 이 회사에 다닌 지 얼마나 됐어요?

usage_en: Say you're still in the middle of doing something. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 아직 밥 먹는 중이에요. 조금만 기다려요. (I'm still eating. Wait just a moment.) or 아직 준비하는 중이에요. 5분만요. (I'm still getting ready. Just 5 more minutes.).

examples.en: I'm still eating. Wait just a moment.
examples.ko: 아직 밥 먹는 중이에요. 조금만 기다려요.

examples.en: I'm still getting ready. Just 5 more minutes.
I'm still thinking about it. I haven't decided yet.
examples.ko: 아직 생각하는 중이에요. 결정 못 했어요.

usage_en: Tell someone you're almost finished with what you're doing. Say what you need, then add 거의 다 됐어요 at the end. Common uses: 조금만 기다려요. 거의 다 됐어요. (Wait just a little. It's almost done.) or 숙제 거의 다 됐어요. 5분만 주세요. (My homework is almost done. Give me 5 minutes.).

examples.en: Wait just a little. It's almost done.
My homework is almost done. Give me 5 minutes.
The food is almost ready. Please take a seat.
examples.ko: 요리 거의 다 됐어요. 자리 앉아요.

usage_en: Ask someone about their preferences in style or taste. Say what you need, then add 스타일 좋아해요 at the end. Common uses: 어떤 음악 스타일 좋아해요? (What music style do you like?) or 캐주얼 스타일 좋아해요, 아니면 포멀 스타일 좋아해요? (Do you prefer casual style or formal style?).

examples.en: What music style do you like?
Do you prefer casual style or formal style?
examples.ko: 캐주얼 스타일 좋아해요, 아니면 포멀 스타일 좋아해요?

examples.en: What interior design style do you like?

usage_en: Compliment someone by saying something suits them really well. Say what you need, then add 잘 어울려요 at the end. Common uses: 그 옷 잘 어울려요! (That outfit suits you really well!) or 그 머리색이 잘 어울려요. (That hair color suits you perfectly.).

examples.en: That outfit suits you really well!
That hair color suits you perfectly.
Those glasses suit you well. You look great.

usage_en: Tell someone something is currently on trend. Say what you need, then add 요즘 유행이에요 at the end. Common uses: 이 색이 요즘 유행이에요. (This color is trending these days.) or 숏폼 영상이 요즘 유행이에요. (Short-form videos are all the rage these days.).

examples.en: This color is trending these days.
Short-form videos are all the rage these days.
This style is really trending now. A lot of people are wearing it.
examples.ko: 이런 스타일이 요즘 유행이에요. 많이들 입어요.

usage_en: Ask how long a delivery will take to arrive. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 배달 얼마나 걸려요? 많이 배고파요. (How long does delivery take? I'm really hungry.) or 이 음식점은 배달 얼마나 걸려요? (How long does delivery take from this restaurant?).

examples.en: How long does delivery take? I'm really hungry.
How long does delivery take from this restaurant?
How long will delivery take? Is it okay to order now?
examples.ko: 배달 얼마나 걸려요? 지금 주문해도 돼요?

usage_en: Say something offers great value for the price paid. Say what you need, then add 가성비 좋아요 at the end. Common uses: 이 식당은 가성비 좋아요. 양도 많아요. (This restaurant is great value. The portions are big too.) or 이 호텔 가성비 좋아요. 추천해요. (This hotel is great value. I recommend it.).

examples.en: This restaurant is great value. The portions are big too.
examples.ko: 이 식당은 가성비 좋아요. 양도 많아요.

examples.en: This hotel is great value. I recommend it.
This product is great value — it's cheap and good quality.
examples.ko: 이 제품은 가성비 좋아요. 싸고 질도 좋아요.

usage_en: Ask if someone has any upcoming travel plans. Say what you need, then add 여행 계획 있어요 at the end. Common uses: 이번 여름에 여행 계획 있어요? (Do you have any travel plans this summer?) or 한국 여행 계획 있어요? 같이 가요! (Do you have plans to travel to Korea? Let's go together!).

examples.en: Do you have any travel plans this summer?
Do you have plans to travel to Korea? Let's go together!
examples.ko: 한국 여행 계획 있어요? 같이 가요!

examples.en: Do you have travel plans? Where do you want to go?
examples.ko: 여행 계획 있어요? 어디 가고 싶어요?

usage_en: Ask how many days someone plans to stay somewhere. Just place a noun before 며칠이나 있을 거예요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 한국에 며칠이나 있을 거예요? (How many days will you be staying in Korea?) or 제주도에 며칠이나 있을 거예요? (How many days are you planning to stay in Jeju?).

examples.en: How many days will you be staying in Korea?
How many days are you planning to stay in Jeju?
How many days will you stay on your trip?

usage_en: Ask for a must-see recommendation when visiting a place. Just place a noun before 꼭 봐야 할 게 뭐예요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 서울에서 꼭 봐야 할 게 뭐예요? (What's a must-see in Seoul?) or 한국에 처음 왔어요. 꼭 봐야 할 게 뭐예요? (It's my first time in Korea. What must I see?).

examples.en: What's a must-see in Seoul?
examples.ko: 서울에서 꼭 봐야 할 게 뭐예요?

examples.en: It's my first time in Korea. What must I see?
examples.ko: 한국에 처음 왔어요. 꼭 봐야 할 게 뭐예요?

examples.en: What's a must-see in this city? Please give me a recommendation.
examples.ko: 이 도시에서 꼭 봐야 할 게 뭐예요? 추천해 주세요.

usage_en: Ask a friend casually how they're finding life in Korea. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 한국 생활 어때? 재미있어? (How's life in Korea? Is it fun?) or 한국 생활 어때? 힘든 점 없어? (How's life in Korea? Is there anything you find hard?).

examples.en: How's life in Korea? Is it fun?
How's life in Korea? Is there anything you find hard?
examples.ko: 한국 생활 어때? 힘든 점 없어?

examples.en: It's been a month since you came to Korea — how's life here?
examples.ko: 한국 온 지 한 달 됐는데, 한국 생활 어때?

usage_en: Tell a friend you've gotten used to something now. Say what you need, then add 이제 익숙해졌어 at the end. Common uses: 처음엔 힘들었는데 이제 익숙해졌어. (It was tough at first, but I'm used to it now.) or 한국 음식 이제 익숙해졌어. 다 잘 먹어. (I'm used to Korean food now. I eat everything.).

examples.en: It was tough at first, but I'm used to it now.
I'm used to Korean food now. I eat everything.
examples.ko: 한국 음식 이제 익숙해졌어. 다 잘 먹어.

examples.en: I'm used to the Seoul subway now. I don't get lost anymore.
examples.ko: 서울 지하철 이제 익숙해졌어. 길 안 잃어버려.

literal_en: Among Korean foods, I like samgyeopsal the ~
usage_en: Tell a friend what you like or enjoy the most. Say what you need, then add 이 제일 좋아 at the end. Common uses: 한국 음식 중에 삼겹살이 제일 좋아. (Among Korean foods, I like samgyeopsal the most.) or 계절 중에 가을이 제일 좋아. (Fall is my favorite season.).

examples.en: Among Korean foods, I like samgyeopsal the most.
examples.ko: 한국 음식 중에 삼겹살이 제일 좋아.

examples.en: Fall is my favorite season.
This song is my favorite. I listen to it every day.
examples.ko: 이 노래가 제일 좋아. 매일 들어.

literal_en: I'm going to meet a friend ~
usage_en: Express future plans or predictions naturally in Korean. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 내일 친구를 만날 거예요. (I'm going to meet a friend tomorrow.) or 이번 주말에 영화 볼 거예요. (I'm going to watch a movie this weekend.).

examples.en: I'm going to meet a friend tomorrow.
I'm going to watch a movie this weekend.
I'm going to go to Korea when I graduate.

literal_en: I'm planning to take a Korean exam next ~
usage_en: Say you intend or are planning to do something soon. Say what you need, then add 려고 해요 at the end. Common uses: 내년에 한국어 시험을 보려고 해요. (I'm planning to take a Korean exam next year.) or 오늘 저녁에 요리하려고 해요. (I'm planning to cook dinner tonight.).

examples.en: I'm planning to take a Korean exam next year.
I'm planning to cook dinner tonight.
I'm planning to clean this weekend.

usage_en: Express what you want or wish to do right now. Say what you need, then add 고 싶어요 at the end. Common uses: 한국에 살고 싶어요. (I want to live in Korea.) or 한국어를 유창하게 말하고 싶어요. (I want to speak Korean fluently.).

examples.en: I want to live in Korea.
I want to speak Korean fluently.
I want to eat something delicious. What should we have?
examples.ko: 맛있는 거 먹고 싶어요. 뭐 먹을까요?

usage_en: Share a decision you've made with someone. Say what you need, then add 기로 했어요 at the end. Common uses: 한국에서 살기로 했어요. (I've decided to live in Korea.) or 내년에 한국어 학원에 다니기로 했어요. (I've decided to attend a Korean language school next year.).

examples.en: I've decided to live in Korea.
I've decided to attend a Korean language school next year.
I've decided to exercise every day starting today.

usage_en: Say you've firmly made up your mind about something. Say what you need, then add 마음먹었어요 at the end. Common uses: 한국어 꼭 잘하기로 마음먹었어요. (I've made up my mind to get really good at Korean.) or 이번엔 포기하지 않기로 마음먹었어요. (I've decided not to give up this time.).

examples.en: I've made up my mind to get really good at Korean.
I've decided not to give up this time.
I've made up my mind to lose weight. I'll exercise starting tomorrow.

usage_en: Say a skill or ability has improved compared to before. Say what you need, then add 예전보다 늘었어요 at the end. Common uses: 한국어 실력이 예전보다 늘었어요. (My Korean has improved compared to before.) or 요리 실력이 예전보다 늘었어요. (My cooking has gotten better than it used to be.).

examples.en: My Korean has improved compared to before.
My cooking has gotten better than it used to be.
My English has improved from before. I've gained confidence.

literal_en: Have you tried bibimbap? It's really ~
usage_en: Casually ask a friend if they've ever tried something. Say what you need, then add 어 봤어 at the end. Common uses: 비빔밥 먹어 봤어? 진짜 맛있어. (Have you tried bibimbap? It's really delicious.) or 한국 드라마 본 적 있어? 재미있어. (Have you watched a Korean drama? It's so fun.).

examples.en: Have you tried bibimbap? It's really delicious.
Have you watched a Korean drama? It's so fun.
examples.ko: 한국 드라마 본 적 있어? 재미있어.

examples.en: Have you tried bungee jumping? Is it scary?

literal_en: Now that I've studied Korean, it's more fun than I ~
usage_en: Share a realization or finding after trying or doing something. Say what you need, then add 보니까 at the end. Common uses: 한국어 공부해 보니까 생각보다 재미있어요. (Now that I've studied Korean, it's more fun than I expected.) or 먹어 보니까 맵지 않아요. (Now that I've tried it, it's not spicy at all.).

examples.en: Now that I've studied Korean, it's more fun than I expected.
Now that I've tried it, it's not spicy at all.
Now that I've lived here, Korea is a great place to live.
examples.ko: 살아 보니까 한국이 정말 살기 좋아요.

literal_en: My friend recommended this restaurant. They say it's ~
usage_en: Tell someone who recommended something to you. Say what you need, then add 추천해줬어 at the end. Common uses: 친구가 이 식당 추천해줬어. 맛있대. (My friend recommended this restaurant. They say it's delicious.) or 선생님이 이 책 추천해줬어. (My teacher recommended this book to me.).

examples.en: My friend recommended this restaurant. They say it's delicious.
My teacher recommended this book to me.
A YouTuber recommended this product. I want to try it.
examples.ko: 유튜버가 이 제품 추천해줬어. 써보고 싶어.

literal_en: Can you teach me this dish? I want to learn how to make ~
usage_en: Casually ask a friend to teach you something. Say what you need, then add 가르쳐줄 수 있어 at the end. Common uses: 이 요리 가르쳐줄 수 있어? 배우고 싶어. (Can you teach me this dish? I want to learn how to make it.) or 한국어 발음 가르쳐줄 수 있어? (Can you teach me Korean pronunciation?).

examples.en: Can you teach me this dish? I want to learn how to make it.
examples.ko: 이 요리 가르쳐줄 수 있어? 배우고 싶어.

examples.en: Can you teach me Korean pronunciation?
Can you teach me guitar? I've wanted to learn for a long time.
examples.ko: 기타 가르쳐줄 수 있어? 오래 배우고 싶었어.

usage_en: Casually check if your understanding or information is correct. Say what you need, then add 맞아 at the end. Common uses: 여기가 홍대역 맞아? (This is Hongdae station, right?) or 내일 2시에 만나는 거 맞아? (We're meeting at 2 o'clock tomorrow, right?).

examples.en: This is Hongdae station, right?
We're meeting at 2 o'clock tomorrow, right?
This is your bag, right? Here it is.
examples.ko: 이거 네 가방 맞아? 여기 있어.

literal_en: How do you use this app? It's my first ~
usage_en: Ask a friend casually how to do or use something. Say what you need, then add 어떻게 해 at the end. Common uses: 이 앱 어떻게 해? 처음 써봐. (How do you use this app? It's my first time.) or 한국에서 배달 주문 어떻게 해? (How do you order delivery in Korea?).

examples.en: How do you use this app? It's my first time.
examples.ko: 이 앱 어떻게 해? 처음 써봐.

examples.en: How do you order delivery in Korea?
How do you play this game? Explain the rules.
examples.ko: 이 게임 어떻게 해? 규칙 알려줘.

literal_en: Have you ever tried making kimchi? Is it ~?
usage_en: Ask a friend if they've ever tried making something themselves. Just place a noun before 만들어봤어 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 김치 만들어봤어? 어려워? (Have you ever tried making kimchi? Is it hard?) or 홈메이드 케이크 만들어봤어? (Have you ever tried making a homemade cake?).

examples.en: Have you ever tried making kimchi? Is it hard?
Have you ever tried making a homemade cake?
Have you tried making your own clothes? That sounds so cool.
examples.ko: 직접 옷 만들어봤어? 멋질 것 같아.

literal_en: How much sugar do you add? I think it'll be too ~
usage_en: Ask how much of an ingredient to add when cooking. Just place a noun before 얼마나 넣어 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 설탕 얼마나 넣어? 너무 달 것 같아. (How much sugar do you add? I think it'll be too sweet.) or 소금 얼마나 넣어? 레시피에 없어. (How much salt do you put in? It's not in the recipe.).

examples.en: How much sugar do you add? I think it'll be too sweet.
examples.ko: 설탕 얼마나 넣어? 너무 달 것 같아.

examples.en: How much salt do you put in? It's not in the recipe.
How much gochujang do you add? Can I make it spicy?
examples.ko: 고추장 얼마나 넣어? 맵게 해도 돼?

usage_en: Tell a friend casually that they just need to do one thing. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 이 버튼 누르면 돼. 쉬워. (Just press this button. It's easy.) or 여기서 왼쪽으로 꺾으면 돼. (Just turn left from here.).

examples.en: Just press this button. It's easy.
Just turn left from here.
Just write your name and phone number.

literal_en: I'm going to buy new sneakers ~
usage_en: Tell someone what you're planning to buy. Say what you need, then add 살 거예요 at the end. Common uses: 오늘 새 운동화 살 거예요. (I'm going to buy new sneakers today.) or 이번 주에 생일 선물 살 거예요. (I'm going to buy a birthday gift this week.).

examples.en: I'm going to buy new sneakers today.
I'm going to buy a birthday gift this week.
examples.ko: 이번 주에 생일 선물 살 거예요.

examples.en: I'm going to buy a laptop when I get my paycheck.

usage_en: Ask for someone's honest opinion on a specific item. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 이 옷 어때요? 저한테 어울려요? (How is this outfit? Does it suit me?) or 이거 어때요? 선물로 괜찮을까요? (How is this? Will it work as a gift?).

examples.en: How is this outfit? Does it suit me?
How is this? Will it work as a gift?
How is this color? Do you like it?

usage_en: Tell a cashier or server you'll be paying by card. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 카드로 할게요. 현금은 없어요. (I'll pay by card. I don't have any cash.) or 카드로 할게요. 신용카드도 돼요? (I'll pay by card. Is a credit card okay?).

examples.en: I'll pay by card. I don't have any cash.
I'll pay by card. Is a credit card okay?
We'll pay separately. I'll pay by card.

literal_en: Have you been to a Korean noraebang? It's really ~
usage_en: Casually ask a friend if they've experienced or tried something. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 한국 노래방 가봤어? 진짜 재미있어. (Have you been to a Korean noraebang? It's really fun.) or 스카이다이빙 해봤어? (Have you tried skydiving?).

examples.en: Have you been to a Korean noraebang? It's really fun.
Have you tried skydiving?
Have you tried traveling alone? I'm curious what it's like.

usage_en: Ask a friend casually how something went or felt. Say what you need, then add 어땠어 at the end. Common uses: 어제 소개팅 어땠어? (How was your blind date yesterday?) or 면접 어땠어? 잘 됐어? (How did the interview go? Did it go well?).

examples.en: How was your blind date yesterday?
How did the interview go? Did it go well?
How was your trip to Korea? Was it fun?

literal_en: I want to receive flowers for my ~
usage_en: Express something you'd like to receive as a gift or gesture. Say what you need, then add 받고 싶어요 at the end. Common uses: 생일에 꽃 받고 싶어요. (I want to receive flowers for my birthday.) or 누군가한테 편지 받고 싶어요. (I want to receive a handwritten letter from someone.).

examples.en: I want to receive flowers for my birthday.
I want to receive a handwritten letter from someone.
I want to receive one warm, kind word.

usage_en: Ask a patient or friend where they're feeling pain. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 어디가 아파요? 병원에 가야 해요? (Where does it hurt? Do you need to go to the hospital?) or 어디가 아파요? 많이 힘들어 보여요. (Where does it hurt? You look like you're suffering a lot.).

examples.en: Where does it hurt? Do you need to go to the hospital?
Where does it hurt? You look like you're suffering a lot.
Where does it hurt? Do you have any medicine?

usage_en: Ask when someone's pain or illness first started. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 언제부터 아팠어요? 어제부터예요? (Since when have you been in pain? Since yesterday?) or 머리가 언제부터 아팠어요? (Since when has your head been hurting?).

examples.en: Since when have you been in pain? Since yesterday?
Since when has your head been hurting?
When did the pain start? You should tell the doctor.

literal_en: Have you been to Jeju Island ~?
usage_en: Ask politely if someone has visited a particular place before. Just place a noun before 와 봤어요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 제주도에 와 봤어요? (Have you been to Jeju Island before?) or 이 카페에 와 봤어요? 처음이에요? (Have you been to this café before? Is it your first time?).

examples.en: Have you been to Jeju Island before?
Have you been to this café before? Is it your first time?
Have you been to Korea before? How was it?

literal_en: This place is great for taking ~
usage_en: Say a place or season is great for doing a particular thing. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 여기 사진 찍기 좋아요. (This place is great for taking photos.) or 이 카페 공부하기 좋아요. 조용해요. (This café is great for studying. It's very quiet.).

examples.en: This place is great for taking photos.
This café is great for studying. It's very quiet.
Spring is a great time for traveling.

usage_en: Ask someone to pick their favorite from a set of options. Say what you need, then add 중에 뭐가 제일 좋아요 at the end. Common uses: 한국 음식 중에 뭐가 제일 좋아요? (What's your favorite among Korean foods?) or 가본 나라 중에 뭐가 제일 좋아요? (Which country you've visited did you like the most?).

examples.en: What's your favorite among Korean foods?
examples.ko: 한국 음식 중에 뭐가 제일 좋아요?

examples.en: Which country you've visited did you like the most?
examples.ko: 가본 나라 중에 뭐가 제일 좋아요?

examples.en: Which season do you like the most?

literal_en: This song is addictive because the melody is so ~
usage_en: Explain exactly why something is so addictive or hard to stop. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 이 노래 멜로디가 좋아서 중독성 있어요. (This song is addictive because the melody is so good.) or 이 음식 매콤해서 중독성 있어요. (This food is addictive because it's perfectly spicy.).

examples.en: This song is addictive because the melody is so good.
examples.ko: 이 노래 멜로디가 좋아서 중독성 있어요.

examples.en: This food is addictive because it's perfectly spicy.
This drama is addictive because the story is so interesting.
examples.ko: 이 드라마 스토리가 재미있어서 중독성 있어요.

literal_en: It's different from my country. So ~
usage_en: Point out how something differs from something else. Say what you need, then add 이랑 달라요 at the end. Common uses: 제 나라이랑 달라요. 신기해요. (It's different from my country. So interesting.) or 생각이랑 달라요. 더 좋아요. (It's different from what I expected. Even better.).

examples.en: It's different from my country. So interesting.
It's different from what I expected. Even better.
It's different from yesterday. Even tastier today.

usage_en: Admit something feels a bit awkward or off without saying it directly. Just place a noun before 좀 그렇긴 한데 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 솔직히 좀 그렇긴 한데, 괜찮아요. (Honestly, it's a little awkward, but it's okay.) or 좀 그렇긴 한데 어떻게 말해야 할지 모르겠어요. (It's a bit off, but I'm not sure how to say it.).

examples.en: Honestly, it's a little awkward, but it's okay.
It's a bit off, but I'm not sure how to say it.
examples.ko: 좀 그렇긴 한데 어떻게 말해야 할지 모르겠어요.

examples.en: It's a bit odd, but I'll just let it go.

usage_en: Ask casually if it's okay to give an honest opinion. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 솔직하게 말해도 돼? 좀 아쉬운 게 있어. (Can I be honest? There's something that disappoints me a little.) or 솔직하게 말해도 돼? 이 옷은 별로야. (Can I be frank? This outfit isn't great.).

examples.en: Can I be honest? There's something that disappoints me a little.
examples.ko: 솔직하게 말해도 돼? 좀 아쉬운 게 있어.

examples.en: Can I be frank? This outfit isn't great.
examples.ko: 솔직하게 말해도 돼? 이 옷은 별로야.

examples.en: Can I be real with you? I think a different approach would be better.
examples.ko: 솔직하게 말해도 돼? 다른 방법이 더 좋을 것 같아.

usage_en: Say something has a quality in a subtle or surprisingly strong way. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 이 음식 은근히 맛있어. (This food is surprisingly good.) or 그 사람 은근히 웃겨. (That person is subtly funny.).

examples.en: This food is surprisingly good.
That person is subtly funny.
This movie is low-key scary.

literal_en: I'm busy because of exams. I'll contact you ~
usage_en: Explain what is keeping you busy right now. Just place a noun before 때문에 바빠요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 시험 때문에 바빠요. 나중에 연락할게요. (I'm busy because of exams. I'll contact you later.) or 프로젝트 때문에 바빠요. (I'm busy because of a project.).

examples.en: I'm busy because of exams. I'll contact you later.
I'm busy because of a project.
I'm busy because of moving preparations.

usage_en: Advise someone not to push themselves too hard. Say what you need, then add 무리하지 마세요 at the end. Common uses: 몸이 안 좋으면 무리하지 마세요. (If you're not feeling well, don't push yourself.) or 무리하지 마세요. 천천히 해도 돼요. (Don't overdo it. It's okay to take it slow.).

examples.en: If you're not feeling well, don't push yourself.
Don't overdo it. It's okay to take it slow.
Don't overexert yourself. Health comes first.

literal_en: Do you exercise a lot? You look ~
usage_en: Ask casually if someone does something frequently or a lot. Just place a noun before 많이 해 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 운동 많이 해? 몸이 좋아 보여. (Do you exercise a lot? You look fit.) or 요리 많이 해? 잘하는 것 같아. (Do you cook a lot? You seem good at it.).

examples.en: Do you exercise a lot? You look fit.
examples.ko: 운동 많이 해? 몸이 좋아 보여.

examples.en: Do you cook a lot? You seem good at it.
examples.ko: 요리 많이 해? 잘하는 것 같아.

examples.en: Do you study Korean a lot? You're really good.
examples.ko: 한국어 공부 많이 해? 진짜 잘하네.

usage_en: Ask if something is currently trendy or popular. Say what you need, then add 유행이야 at the end. Common uses: 요즘 이 스타일 유행이야? (Is this style trendy these days?) or 이 노래 유행이야? 어디서 많이 들려. (Is this song popular? I keep hearing it everywhere.).

examples.en: Is this style trendy these days?
Is this song popular? I keep hearing it everywhere.
examples.ko: 이 노래 유행이야? 어디서 많이 들려.

examples.en: Is this food a trend? I keep seeing it on social media.
examples.ko: 이 음식 유행이야? SNS에 자주 나오던데.

literal_en: After I posted the photo, I got a lot of ~
usage_en: Share what happened after you posted or uploaded something online. Just place a noun before 올렸더니 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 사진 올렸더니 댓글이 많이 달렸어. (After I posted the photo, I got a lot of comments.) or 영상 올렸더니 반응이 좋았어. (After I uploaded the video, the response was great.).

examples.en: After I posted the photo, I got a lot of comments.
After I uploaded the video, the response was great.
After I posted a food photo, lots of people asked for the recipe.
examples.ko: 요리 사진 올렸더니 레시피 물어보는 사람이 많았어.

literal_en: I'm going to take on cooking this ~
usage_en: Announce you're taking on a new challenge or trying something for the first time. Say what you need, then add 도전해요 at the end. Common uses: 이번 주에 요리 도전해요. (I'm going to take on cooking this week.) or 혼자 여행 도전해요. (I'm challenging myself to travel alone.).

examples.en: I'm going to take on cooking this week.
I'm challenging myself to travel alone.
I'm going to challenge myself with the Korean exam!

usage_en: Check if the necessary ingredients are available. Say what you need, then add 재료가 있어요 at the end. Common uses: 김치찌개 만들려는데, 재료가 있어요? (I want to make kimchi stew — do you have the ingredients?) or 재료가 있어요? 없으면 마트 가야 해요. (Do you have the ingredients? If not, we need to go to the store.).

examples.en: I want to make kimchi stew — do you have the ingredients?
Do you have the ingredients? If not, we need to go to the store.
examples.ko: 재료가 있어요? 없으면 마트 가야 해요.

examples.en: I have all the ingredients at home. I can make it right away.
examples.ko: 집에 재료가 있어요. 바로 만들 수 있어요.

usage_en: Encourage yourself or someone else that next time will be better. Say what you need, then add 다음엔 더 잘할 거예요 at the end. Common uses: 이번엔 실수했지만 다음엔 더 잘할 거예요. (I made a mistake this time, but next time I'll do better.) or 괜찮아요. 다음엔 더 잘할 거예요. (It's okay. Next time will be better.).

examples.en: I made a mistake this time, but next time I'll do better.
examples.ko: 이번엔 실수했지만 다음엔 더 잘할 거예요.

examples.en: It's okay. Next time will be better.
Don't give up. You'll do better next time.
examples.ko: 포기하지 말아요. 다음엔 더 잘할 거예요.

literal_en: Do you have a morning routine? How do you start your ~?
usage_en: Ask if someone has a regular habit or routine for something. Just place a noun before 루틴 있어요 — no conjugation needed. Common uses: 아침 루틴 있어요? 어떻게 시작해요? (Do you have a morning routine? How do you start your day?) or 스킨케어 루틴 있어요? (Do you have a skincare routine?).

examples.en: Do you have a morning routine? How do you start your day?
Do you have a skincare routine?
Do you have a workout routine? I'd love to follow it.
examples.ko: 운동 루틴 있어요? 따라해 보고 싶어요.

usage_en: Say what you plan to do or did after completing an action. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 밥 먹고 나서 같이 산책해요. (Let's take a walk after eating.) or 일 끝나고 나서 연락할게요. (I'll contact you after I finish work.).

examples.en: Let's take a walk after eating.
I'll contact you after I finish work.
Let's talk after I shower.

usage_en: Insist that something absolutely must be done. It works in casual and polite speech alike. Common uses: 한국에 오면 삼겹살 꼭 먹어야 해요. (If you come to Korea, you absolutely have to eat samgyeopsal.) or 이 카페 꼭 가봐야 해요. (You absolutely have to visit this café.).

examples.en: If you come to Korea, you absolutely have to eat samgyeopsal.
examples.ko: 한국에 오면 삼겹살 꼭 먹어야 해요.

examples.en: You absolutely have to visit this café.
You absolutely must follow the rules.
